text: Chapter 15, designing Google Drive. Let's see how it works in a few minutes.

A cloud drive is really two systems. File contents are cut into blocks and kept in block storage in the cloud. Everything small and fast-changing, like the file name, its list of blocks, and its version number, lives in a metadata database. Contents are big, the directory is small, so we store them apart and scale each one on its own.

First, how a file is stored. It's cut into blocks of at most four megabytes. Each block gets a hash, which acts as its unique ID. Put the hashes in order, and you have the file's block list. To rebuild the file, just follow the list and join the blocks together.

If only a small part of a file changes, we shouldn't upload all of it. The client splits the file locally, computes the hashes, and sends the new block list to the server. The server compares it and answers: only block three is missing. So the client uploads just that block, and the rest reuse the old ones. This is delta sync, and it saves the client's upload bandwidth.

Blocks are named by their hash, so identical blocks are stored only once. Different files and different versions can all point to the same block. That's deduplication. Data is also compressed before upload, though images and video are already compressed, so the gain is small. When an old version is deleted, we check whether anyone still references a block. Only unreferenced blocks, past the retention period, can be reclaimed.

An upload isn't a single step. First, the metadata records the new version as pending, and other devices can't see it. Blocks arrive one by one. Once the block list and checksums are verified, the status becomes uploaded, and a notification goes out. If the connection drops, the version stays pending, and the blocks already uploaded don't need to be sent again.

Device A has finished uploading. How does device B find out? The notification service uses long polling. B keeps a request hanging, and the moment something changes, the server answers. B then fetches the latest metadata from the API server, downloads only the blocks it's missing, and puts them together in order. If B was offline, the change waits in an offline backup queue until B comes back.

What if two devices edit the same file at the same time? Every commit carries the version it was based on. The server handles the first one, which succeeds, and the version becomes two. The second one is based on the old version one, so it's a conflict. The system never overwrites silently. It keeps both copies and lets the user merge them, or replace one with the other.
Remember three words: chunking, delta, and conflict copies. Contents are stored as blocks, and the directory is managed separately. Send only the changed blocks, and keep a copy when edits conflict.
